say.text: Worked case first. A 40-year-old man has chronic haemolysis from hereditary spherocytosis, and gallstones. Which stone is he most likely to have?

choices.label: Brown pigment stones, forming in the bile ducts
Pure cholesterol stones, the commonest type in texts
Black pigment stones, forming in the gallbladder
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Chronic haemolysis is the clue: black pigment stones are small, multiple and hard, form in the gallbladder, and go with cirrhosis.

Worked through, step by step. Step one: the cause in the stem is chronic haemolysis. Step two: the stone that goes with it is black, formed in the gallbladder. Step three: it goes with cirrhosis, so check the liver.
That is not the right choice. Brown stones tempt you because they are the other pigment type, and they sit in the ducts.
But brown stones are soft and earthy, and go with biliary infection and parasites, not with chronic haemolysis.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this needs a second look: brown stones go with infected bile, not with haemolysis.

say.text: That is not the right choice. The textbook answer tempts, since many Western texts call cholesterol the commonest type.
But the stem gives a haemolytic cause, and pure cholesterol stones are large, solitary and pale, with no link to haemolysis.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the exam key against the texts: they do not give the same answer for 'most common'.

say.text: Start with the cause in the stem. Then ask which stone type goes with that cause, and where it forms.
Case two, with the first step done for you: the bile is infected and the stone is in the duct. Which stone fits?

choices.label: Brown pigment stones, from bile infection
Black pigment stones, from bile infection
Brown pigment stones, from chronic haemolysis
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Soft, earthy stones in the ducts go with biliary infection, and bacterial β-glucuronidase helps them form.
That is not the right choice. Black stones tempt, since infection and pigment stones are often remembered together.
But black stones are small and hard, form in the gallbladder, and go with chronic haemolysis, not with infected bile.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look again: black stones and infected bile belong to different causes.

say.text: That is not the right choice. Brown stones tempt, since they are the stones of the ducts, and haemolysis sounds like a pigment cause.
But chronic haemolysis is the cause tied to black stones, which form in the gallbladder.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look again at which cause goes with which stone.

say.text: Ask what infects the bile, and where the stone sits. Then match the stone to its cause.
The answer is brown pigment stones. They are soft and earthy, form in the bile ducts, and go with infection and stasis.
Exam question: which is the most common gallstone type? Your answer is scored against the PYQ key.

choices.label: Pure cholesterol stones, as texts say
Mixed stones, as the PYQ key expects
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. PYQs have expected mixed stones, while texts group cholesterol and mixed together as the majority.
Cholesterol stones are large and solitary, with risk from female sex, oestrogens, obesity and rapid weight loss.
Cue: female, fat, fertile, forty.
That is not the right choice. The textbook answer tempts, since Western texts call cholesterol the commonest type.
But the exam key follows the PYQ convention, and the texts group cholesterol with mixed stones.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the exam key first: here the PYQ key and the textbook answer differ.

say.text: Separate what the examiner scores from what current texts say. Here the PYQ key and the texts may not match.
The answer is mixed stones, as PYQs expect. Texts group cholesterol and mixed stones together as the majority, about 80%.
A burns patient in the ICU has a sick gallbladder, and imaging finds no stone. Compared with stone-related cholecystitis, is this milder or worse?

choices.label: Milder, since no stone blocks the duct
Worse, with more gangrene and perforation
Milder, since the wall is rarely inflamed
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Acalculous disease runs on stasis and ischaemia in sick patients, and it has more gangrene, perforation and deaths.
That is not the right choice. Stone-free disease tempts, since a stone is the usual cause of the trouble.
But acalculous cholecystitis is driven by stasis and ischaemia, not by a blocked duct, so no stone does not mean mild.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look at what drives the inflammation: stasis and ischaemia, not a stone.

say.text: That is not the right choice. Calm-looking disease tempts, since a gallbladder with no stone seems less inflamed.
But stasis and ischaemia injure the wall in sick patients, and that injury is what goes on to gangrene.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look again at the wall: in these patients it is injured, not spared.

say.text: Ask what drives the inflammation when no stone blocks the duct, and who gets this disease.
The answer is worse. Acalculous cholecystitis comes from stasis and ischaemia after surgery, trauma, burns or sepsis.
It has more gangrene and perforation than calculous disease, and a higher mortality.
